title: The New Primitives: Building AI Native Software — Kwindla Kramer, Daily

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: The talk's central thesis is that agents are a transient primitive (like web pages in 1995) and that fully AI native software is what comes next. It discusses multimodal harnesses (Nadella clip), agent system primitives (long-running subagents sharing context, progressive skills loading), and Gradient Bang as a system exercising these agent architecture patterns at scale with hundreds of concurrent inference calls.

secondary.label: Multimodal & Realtime Systems
secondary.rationale: The speaker leads Daily and Pipecat, the most widely used open-source voice agent framework. Conversational voice is one of the five AI native primitives. The talk traces multimodal computing from Vannevar Bush through the web to modern voice agents, and Gradient Bang features conversational voice as a core interaction modality.

secondary.label: Context Engineering & Memory
secondary.rationale: Asynchronous non-blocking context compression is explicitly named as one of the five AI native software primitives demonstrated in Gradient Bang. The Nadella clip discusses progressive tool disclosure for token efficiency, which is a context engineering pattern. The talk argues these context management primitives define the next era of agent systems.

secondary.label: AI Product, UX & Human Factors
secondary.rationale: The talk traces the evolution of computing interfaces (Sketchpad, VisiCalc, Knowledge Navigator, Minority Report gestural UI, Iron Man JARVIS) and argues that dynamic interface generation is a key AI native primitive. The historical arc is partly about human-computer interaction paradigms and how interface abstractions transformed work.

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk is a cross-domain vision about the future of AI native software, drawing from eighty years of computing history without focusing on a single application vertical. The argument applies broadly to all AI engineering.

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: Pipecat is a developer framework for building voice agents, and the talk implicitly addresses what developer primitives will be needed for AI native software. The five named primitives (context compression, subagents, skills loading, dynamic UI, voice) are developer-facing capabilities.

domains.label: Media & Creative
domains.rationale: Gradient Bang is a creative/gaming application demonstrating AI native primitives, and the talk discusses creative computing history including Hollywood interface design from Minority Report and Iron Man based on real MIT Media Lab research.

domains.label: Personal Productivity
domains.rationale: The historical vision of personal computing assistants (Knowledge Navigator, Memex, Jarvis) frames the talk's vision of future AI assistants as personal productivity tools that are now buildable on real infrastructure.

summary:
Kwindla Kramer, CEO and co-founder of Daily, delivers a keynote tracing eighty years of computing history to argue that AI agents are a transient primitive—not a destination—and that fully AI native software is what comes next. He introduces Pipecat, the most widely used open-source, vendor-neutral voice agent framework, adopted by AWS, Nvidia, Anthropic, and thousands of startups. Drawing a parallel between his 1995 excitement as a web programmer and today's agent developers, he frames agents as the web pages of this era: a starting primitive that will evolve into something richer.

The talk walks through computing's decade-by-decade evolution: Vannevar Bush's 1945 "As We May Think" essay predicted OCR, hypertext, search engines, and voice interfaces at the dawn of computing; the 1950s focused on programming languages and compilers; the 1960s on interactivity, Sutherland's Sketchpad, and science fiction (Star Trek, HAL 9000); the 1970s on scaling abstractions like relational databases, declarative languages, and OOP; the 1980s on personal computing (Macintosh 1984, VisiCalc); the 1990s on the web—consciously multimodal from inception; the 2000s on mobile and screen futurism; the 2010s on cloud infrastructure. Each decade's primitives became transformative platforms. VisiCalc didn't eliminate accounting—it expanded it massively, a counter-argument to AI-driven mass unemployment fears.

Kramer highlights Hollywood UI visions rooted in real research: John Underkoffler's MIT Media Lab PhD work inspired gestural interfaces in Minority Report (2002) and Iron Man. Kramer co-founded Oblong Industries with Underkoffler in 2006 to commercialize these interfaces. Apple's 1987 Knowledge Navigator concept video similarly anticipated today's AI assistants. A Nadella clip from a podcast crossover describes current agent engineering as building multimodal harnesses with progressive tool disclosure for token efficiency—labeled "agents plus plus."

The talk closes with Gradient Bang, an open-source massively multiplayer game with LLMs at the core of every interaction—hundreds of concurrent inference calls, impossible even a year ago. It exercises five AI native software primitives: asynchronous non-blocking context compression, long-running subagents sharing context, progressive skills loading, dynamic interface generation, and conversational voice. Kramer argues these primitives define what comes after agents, just as the modern internet is to the web pages of 1995.
whyItMatters: These concepts form a coherent narrative arc that connects computing history to the future of AI engineering. The software engineering concepts (progressive tool disclosure, async context compression, subagent orchestration, dynamic UI generation, voice agent loops, vendor-neutral frameworks, multimodal design) describe the concrete technical primitives that constitute AI native software—the implementation layer. The AI concepts (AI native software, agents as transient primitive, multimodal harnesses, progressive skills loading, Memex vision, VisiCalc precedent, conversational voice, historical abstractions arc) provide the conceptual framing and strategic vision—the why and what-for. Together, they answer two linked questions: what comes after agents (AI native software with five specific primitives), and why we should believe this trajectory (eighty years of computing history showing that each era's primitives evolved into transformative platforms that expanded rather than eliminated work). The talk's unique contribution is synthesizing historical analysis with a working technical demonstration—Gradient Bang—that exercises all five named primitives in production, making the conceptual claims concrete and testable rather than purely speculative. Pipecat and Gradient Bang serve as the bridge between vision and implementation, showing that the infrastructure now exists to build the long-envisioned assistants for real.
temporalContext: The video was published on August 7, 2026, and research was conducted as of August 23, 2026. The talk was delivered in mid-2026, a period when Pipecat had recently reached Cloud GA (January 2026) and Gradient Bang was actively in development (speaker's blog post about it dated May 15, 2026). The talk situates itself within an eighty-year arc of computing history (1945–2026) and argues that the current moment—when agents are mainstream but AI native software is just emerging—is analogous to 1995, when web pages were new but the full internet era had not yet arrived. Key external temporal markers: Pipecat Cloud GA (Jan 2026), Gradient Bang subagent patterns blog post (May 2026), Apple Knowledge Navigator video (1987), Vannevar Bush's "As We May Think" essay (1945), Minority Report film (2002), Iron Man film (2008), Oblong Industries co-founded (2006), TaoWeave name change (Dec 2025).
takeaways: Agents are the web pages of this era—a primitive, not a destination; fully AI native software is what comes next

Pipecat is the most widely used open-source, vendor-neutral framework for building voice agents, used by AWS, Nvidia, Anthropic, and thousands of companies

Hollywood futurism from the 2000s—Minority Report and Iron Man—was based on real MIT Media Lab research and has driven decades of commercial interface work
We now have the infrastructure to build the Memex, Jarvis, and Knowledge Navigator for real, using actual available technology

concepts.name: AI native software
concepts.explanation: The conceptual successor to current agent paradigms, analogous to how today's internet is to the web pages of 1995. Not merely agents embedded in existing software, but software architected around AI at its core, where every interaction is mediated by LLM inference and the interface, logic, and content are emergent from agent behavior.
concepts.importance: This is the central thesis of the talk—the answer to 'what comes after agents.' It provides the conceptual frame for all five named primitives and for understanding how agent systems will evolve beyond current harnesses and copilots.

concepts.name: Agents as transient primitive
concepts.explanation: The thesis that AI agents today are like web pages in 1995: a fundamental starting point, not a final destination. Just as web pages evolved into web applications, native mobile apps, and the modern internet, agents will evolve into richer paradigms—specifically, fully AI native software.
concepts.importance: Reframes current agent engineering from an end-state to a beginning, shifting the strategic question from 'how to build better agents' to 'what primitives will define the paradigm that replaces agents as the dominant form.'

concepts.name: Multimodal harnesses ('agents plus plus')
concepts.explanation: The current state-of-the-art agent engineering approach, described via a Nadella podcast clip, where multiple models, data sources, and tools are combined into a single harness with progressive tool disclosure for token efficiency. Includes software copilots embedded across products and organization-level agent harnesses.
concepts.importance: Defines the transitional paradigm between simple single-model agents and fully AI native software. Understanding this intermediate stage is essential for seeing why the five AI native primitives represent a meaningful advance beyond current agent engineering.

concepts.name: Progressive skills loading
concepts.explanation: The capability to dynamically add new skills and tools to an agent at runtime without interrupting real-time interactions. Named as one of five AI native primitives demonstrated in Gradient Bang, enabling agents to acquire new capabilities contextually as the situation demands.
concepts.importance: Represents a shift from static agent configurations to adaptive systems that grow in capability during use, a key differentiator between 'agents plus plus' and true AI native software.

concepts.name: Memex and long-envisioned AI assistant visions
concepts.explanation: Vannevar Bush's 1945 Memex concept—a personal knowledge augmentation device that anticipated OCR, hypertext, search engines, and voice interfaces—alongside Apple's 1987 Knowledge Navigator and Iron Man's JARVIS. Kramer argues these decades-old visions are now buildable on real, available technology.
concepts.importance: Provides the historical grounding for the talk's forward-looking thesis, connecting today's AI native primitives to an eighty-year arc of computing visions and demonstrating that the infrastructure has finally caught up to the imagination.

concepts.name: Technology expanding rather than eliminating work (VisiCalc precedent)
concepts.explanation: The historical pattern exemplified by VisiCalc, the first spreadsheet, which did not eliminate accounting work but made vastly more accounting possible and created new job categories. Kramer offers this as a counter-argument to fears of AI-driven mass unemployment.
concepts.importance: Provides a reasoned framework for evaluating AI's economic impact, grounded in a well-documented historical precedent rather than speculation. Relevant to anyone making strategic decisions about AI adoption and workforce planning.

concepts.name: Conversational voice as AI interaction primitive
concepts.explanation: Conversational voice is named as one of the five AI native software primitives and is central to both Pipecat's architecture and Gradient Bang's design. It represents a foundational modality for AI native software, not an add-on capability.
concepts.importance: Positions voice as a core architectural concern for AI native systems rather than a peripheral interface, with implications for system design, latency budgets, and the coordination of inference loads across modalities.

concepts.name: Historical arc of computing abstractions
concepts.explanation: The decade-by-decade progression where each era's foundational abstractions—programming languages (1950s), interactivity (1960s), relational databases and OOP (1970s), personal computing (1980s), the web (1990s), mobile (2000s), cloud (2010s)—became transformative platforms that expanded rather than replaced prior work.
concepts.importance: Provides the analytical framework for predicting that AI agents and AI native software will follow the same pattern of becoming transformative platforms, using historical evidence rather than hype to argue the trajectory.

concepts.name: Progressive tool disclosure for token efficiency
concepts.explanation: A pattern where an agent's available tools are revealed incrementally rather than all at once, controlling token consumption while maintaining capability. Described by Nadella in a podcast clip as a core current agent engineering approach where the harness defines models, data, and tools with progressive disclosure for token efficiency.
concepts.importance: Represents the current state-of-the-art agent engineering pattern that the talk frames as 'agents plus plus'—the transitional approach between simple agents and fully AI native software.

concepts.name: Asynchronous non-blocking context compression
concepts.explanation: A primitive where long conversation context is compressed in the background without blocking the real-time interaction loop. Named as one of five AI native primitives demonstrated in Gradient Bang, where hundreds of inference calls are in flight at every moment.
concepts.importance: Directly addresses the scalability challenge of maintaining long-running agent conversations with bounded context windows, a core engineering problem for production voice and multimodal agents.

concepts.name: Subagent orchestration with shared context
concepts.explanation: An architectural pattern where multiple LLM-driven subagents run in parallel, sharing conversational context while a primary voice agent maintains the real-time loop. Gradient Bang demonstrates this with a class-based event bus coordinating background task agents running open-ended missions alongside the voice interaction.
concepts.importance: This pattern is central to scaling agent systems beyond single-turn interactions, enabling multi-tasking agent architectures that the talk argues will define AI native software.

concepts.name: Dynamic interface generation from structured LLM output
concepts.explanation: A pattern where the LLM generates structured JSON that is rendered as a dynamic UI on the client side. Gradient Bang's React frontend is rendered from LLM-generated JSON, allowing the interface to adapt in real time to agent decisions and game state.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates how UI generation can be driven by agent reasoning rather than predefined templates, a key primitive for AI native software where the interface itself is an emergent property of agent behavior.

concepts.name: Vendor-neutral open-source framework architecture
concepts.explanation: Pipecat's design as a vendor-neutral Python framework that abstracts transport layers (Daily WebRTC, WebSocket, telephony, LiveKit) and supports multiple AI model providers, allowing developers to build real-time voice and multimodal agents without lock-in.
concepts.importance: Establishes the infrastructure layer that enables the AI native primitives the talk advocates for, providing a portable foundation for building voice agents at scale with hundreds of concurrent inference calls.

concepts.name: Multimodal system design from inception
concepts.explanation: The architectural principle that text, audio, video, and data should be unified from the very beginning of a platform's design, as demonstrated by the web's original multimodal specification and applied to AI native systems where voice, vision, and text are co-designed.
concepts.importance: Provides the design philosophy that Kramer argues should guide AI native software development, treating multimodality as foundational rather than additive, with implications for how voice agent and multimodal AI systems are architected.

concepts.name: Real-time voice agent loop pipeline
concepts.explanation: The end-to-end pipeline where speech-to-text, LLM inference, and text-to-speech must complete within low latency budgets (under 1.5 seconds in Gradient Bang), requiring non-blocking subagent execution and careful orchestration of inference calls.
concepts.importance: Defines the latency constraint that shapes all other architectural decisions in real-time voice agent systems, from context compression strategies to subagent coordination patterns.

sections.title: Introduction and Pipecat
sections.summary: Kramer introduces himself, Daily (real-time audio/video/AI infrastructure), and Pipecat (open-source, vendor-neutral voice agent framework used by AWS, Nvidia, Anthropic, and thousands of startups). He previews the talk: what agents we build today and what comes next, contextualized in eighty years of computing history.

sections.title: As We May Think (1945)
sections.summary: Vannevar Bush's essay predicted document display, scanning, OCR, speech-to-text, programming languages, hypertext, search engines, data networks, a GoPro-like camera, a Kindle-store-like system, voice interfaces, and brain-computer interfaces at the dawn of computing. Kramer draws a parallel between Bush's position at the beginning of computing and our position at the beginning of the intelligence age.

sections.title: Nadella on Multimodal Harnesses and Agents Plus Plus
sections.summary: A Nadella clip describes building multimodal harnesses with tool access, progressive disclosure for token efficiency, and rich context across products like GitHub Copilot and security copilot. Kramer labels this 'agents plus plus'—multi-model harnesses, software copilots embedded everywhere, and organization-level harnesses—and asks how to move beyond agents to the next thing.

sections.title: Web Pages as the Primitive of 1995
sections.summary: Kramer compares his 1995 excitement hand-writing HTML and building web servers in C to today's excitement about agents. Web pages were important but evolved into web and native mobile applications. Agents are the web pages of this era; fully AI native software is what comes after.

sections.title: Computing Timeline: Abacus to AI Agents
sections.summary: Bush's timeline from abacus to electromechanical calculators to the arithmetical machine and the memex. Kramer modifies it: stored program computer, then forty years to the personal computer, then forty years to the AI agents era.

sections.title: 1950s–1960s: Programming Languages and Interactivity
sections.summary: The 1950s focused on programming languages and compilers, combining mathematical formalisms with natural language. The 1960s brought interactivity, two-way human-computer dialogue, Sutherland's Sketchpad, and science fiction influences—Star Trek's conversational computer and Kubrick's HAL 9000.

sections.title: 1970s–1980s: Scaling Abstractions and the Personal Computer
sections.summary: The 1970s delivered relational databases, declarative languages, Smalltalk, and object-oriented programming. The 1980s delivered the personal computer—Macintosh 1984, Windows 1.0 1985—fulfilling Microsoft's mission of a computer on every desk and in every home.

sections.title: VisiCalc and the Unemployment Counter-Argument
sections.summary: VisiCalc, the first spreadsheet, didn't eliminate accountants—it made vastly more accounting possible and created new categories of work that were previously inconceivable. Kramer offers this as a counter-argument to fears of AI-driven mass unemployment.

sections.title: Knowledge Navigator (Apple, 1987)
sections.summary: Apple's concept video predicted a foldable tablet, touchscreen, conversational voice assistant with personality, real-time video generation, computer vision, seamless video calls, autonomous task delegation, and continual learning—updated from Bush's vision for forty years of progress and presaging the AI agent era.

sections.title: The Web Was Multimodal From the Start
sections.summary: The 1990s brought networks and the web. Kramer emphasizes the web was consciously multimodal from the beginning—text, audio, video, and data belonged together. The 2000s made computing mobile and continually connected. The web was an attempt to make the Knowledge Navigator vision real.

sections.title: Mobile Computing and Screen Futurism
sections.summary: The 2000s put a supercomputer in everyone's pocket and, aided by Moore's law for pixels making screens cheap, sparked an efflorescence of futurist imagination on screen. Computers you could carry, cameras everywhere, and cheap screens gave people a new way to think through what the future would look like.

sections.title: Minority Report and Iron Man: Hollywood UI
sections.summary: John Underkoffler created the iconic computer interfaces for Minority Report (2002) and Iron Man, based on his real MIT Media Lab PhD work. Minority Report's gestural interface brought UI out of the small screen and into the physical world. Iron Man offered a different, more optimistic Star Trek-style vision but shared common UI elements. Kramer co-founded a startup with Underkoffler in 2006 to commercialize the Minority Report interface, showing a 2012 demo reel—six years into that work.

sections.title: Cloud, Then Agents, Then What
sections.summary: The 2010s built out the cloud, laying groundwork for the infrastructure and data capacity needed to scale AI training and inference. Now we build agents and are starting to think about agents plus plus. But we can also think about AI native software—to agents what today's internet is to the web pages of 1995. The arc runs from calculator to computer to personal computer to global cloud computer, and now we can build the Memex, Jarvis, and Knowledge Navigator for real.

sections.title: Reimagined Knowledge Navigator on Real Technology
sections.summary: The Tavis team released a reimagined Knowledge Navigator video built entirely on real, available technology. The full four-minute video is one continuous take. It feels both familiar—echoing the 1987 Apple concept—and brand new, demonstrating that the long-envisioned conversational assistant is now buildable.

sections.title: Gradient Bang: AI Native Software in Practice
sections.summary: Kramer closes with Gradient Bang, a massively multiplayer game built from the ground up with LLMs at the core of every interaction, with hundreds of inference calls in flight at every moment—impossible even a year ago. It exercises five AI native primitives: asynchronous non-blocking context compression, long-running subagents that share context, progressive skills loading, dynamic interface generation, and conversational voice. Kramer invites further conversation at the Daily booth and online.

organization.name: Daily
organization.summary: Daily is a real-time voice, video, and AI infrastructure company founded in 2016, headquartered in San Francisco, California. The company builds developer-grade real-time communication infrastructure (WebRTC, audio, video) and maintains Pipecat, the leading open-source framework for voice and multimodal conversational AI agents. Daily serves customers from startups to Fortune 500 and is a W3C WebRTC Working Group member. Pipecat Cloud reached general availability in January 2026, confirming the framework's production maturity and broad adoption by NVIDIA, AWS, all foundation AI labs, and thousands of startups.
organization.status: Active and independent. Pipecat Cloud reached general availability in January 2026. Daily continues to maintain the Pipecat open-source framework (~13,966 GitHub stars) and build real-time AI infrastructure. No acquisition or ownership changes detected.

technologies.label: Pipecat Voice Agent Framework
technologies.summary: Pipecat is the most widely used open-source, vendor-neutral Python framework for building real-time voice and multimodal conversational AI agents, maintained by Daily and a community of over 250 contributors. It is adopted by AWS, Nvidia, all foundation AI labs, and thousands of startups. Pipecat provides the infrastructure layer for the AI native software primitives the talk advocates, enabling real-time voice agent loops, subagent orchestration, and multimodal interactions with hundreds of concurrent inference calls. Pipecat Cloud, the managed deployment platform, reached general availability in January 2026.
technologies.role: Pipecat is introduced at the start of the talk as the speaker's primary contribution to the AI ecosystem—the most widely used open-source framework for building voice agents. It serves as both the practical foundation for Gradient Bang and the conceptual infrastructure for AI native software primitives.

technologies.label: Gradient Bang AI Native Game
technologies.summary: Gradient Bang is an open-source, massively multiplayer online game with LLMs at the core of every interaction, built on Pipecat, Daily WebRTC, Supabase, and Vercel. It demonstrates five AI native software primitives: asynchronous non-blocking context compression, long-running subagents sharing context, progressive skills loading, dynamic interface generation from LLM-generated JSON, and conversational voice. With hundreds of inference calls in flight at every moment, it would have been impossible to build even a year prior to the talk. It serves as a practical validation of the talk's thesis about what comes after agents.
technologies.role: Gradient Bang is the talk's closing demonstration, presented as concrete proof that the five AI native software primitives can be exercised today. It validates the thesis that AI native software is achievable and that the infrastructure has caught up to decades-old visions.

technologies.label: Daily Real-time Media Platform
technologies.summary: Daily is the real-time voice, video, and AI infrastructure company founded by Kwindla Kramer in 2016. As a W3C WebRTC Working Group member, Daily provides the transport and media layer that powers Pipecat and its ecosystem of voice and multimodal agents. The platform serves developers from startups to Fortune 500 companies and is the organizational home for both Pipecat and Gradient Bang.
technologies.role: Daily is introduced as the speaker's company at the start of the talk, providing the real-time infrastructure that underlies Pipecat and all the AI native primitives discussed. It is the organizational and infrastructural context for the entire talk.

technologies.label: AI Native Software Architecture
technologies.summary: AI Native Software Architecture is the central thesis of the talk—the architectural paradigm that comes after agents, analogous to how the modern internet is to the web pages of 1995. It comprises five concrete primitives: asynchronous non-blocking context compression, long-running subagents that share context, progressive skills loading, dynamic interface generation from LLM output, and conversational voice. These primitives are demonstrated in production through Gradient Bang, which exercises all five simultaneously with hundreds of concurrent inference calls. The architecture is enabled by Pipecat as its infrastructure framework and the Pipecat Subagents Library for parallel agent coordination.
technologies.role: AI Native Software Architecture is the talk's central thesis and answer to 'what comes after agents.' The five primitives are named in the final section and then demonstrated through Gradient Bang, making the conceptual claims concrete and testable rather than purely speculative.
